label: subject marker
meaning_en: The subject particle “이/가”: it marks the subject of a sentence, and in particular puts the focus on the subject itself: new information, the answer to “who/what”, or a described state. It also marks the complement of “되다” and “아니다”.
usage: After a consonant it is “이”, after a vowel “가”: “책이, 지수가”. Some pronouns change: “나 → 내가, 저 → 제가, 너 → 네가, 누구 → 누가”. It introduces new information (“옛날 옛적에 호랑이가 살았어요”), answers a question word (“누가 왔어요?”), and marks the subject of descriptions (“비가 와요”). With “좋다”, “싫다”, “필요하다” and “있다/없다” of possession, the thing wanted or had also takes “이/가” (“저는 한국어가 재미있어요”). Double subjects are common: “코끼리는 코가 길다”. Honorific subjects take “께서”.

examples.en: Jisu went to school.
Who opened this window?
It is raining.
I find Korean interesting.
This time I will do it.
An elephant's trunk is long.

compare.difference: “이/가” focuses on the subject: new information or an answer to “who”. “은/는” makes it the topic, with the known or contrasted thing.
“께서” is the honorific “이/가”: with the verb in “-시-”.

pitfalls.note: “나, 저, 너” change before “가”: “내가, 제가, 네가”.
New information (a new character) takes “이/가”, not “은/는”.
pitfalls.en: Once upon a time, a tiger lived.

topik_tip: Questions with “누가/무엇이” are answered with “이/가”: the answer is the subject in focus.

label: and; with
meaning_en: A particle that joins nouns (“A and B”) and marks a partner or comparison (“with, as”): “친구와 함께, 한국과 일본, 이것과 같다”. It is the written, neutral form of “하고” and “이랑”.
usage: After a consonant it is “과”, after a vowel “와”: “책과 연필, 사과와 배”. Listing: “N과 N”. Partner: with reciprocal verbs (“만나다, 싸우다, 결혼하다, 이야기하다, 헤어지다”) the partner takes “와/과” (“친구와 싸우다”). Comparison: “N과 같다/다르다/비슷하다”. “N과 함께” means “together with N”. It sounds written or formal, while speech prefers “하고/이랑”.

examples.en: I study Korean and English.
I watched a movie with a friend.
This outfit is different in color from that one.
Jisu quarreled with Minjun yesterday.
Korea and Japan are close neighbors.

compare.difference: “과/와” and “하고” are near-synonyms; “하고” is the neutral spoken form and attaches to any noun.
With verbs of talking, “와/과” means “with” (a conversation), “에게” means “to” (telling).

pitfalls.note: After a consonant the form is “과”.
pitfalls.en: Korea and Japan are close neighbors.

pitfalls.note: The partner of a reciprocal verb takes “와/과”, not “을/를”.

topik_tip: The partner of “만나다, 싸우다, 결혼하다” takes “와/과” (or “하고/이랑”), not “을/를”.

label: until, up to, even
meaning_en: A particle for the endpoint of a time or place range: “until, up to, as far as”. With a deadline verb it means “by”, and after a noun that is the last in a series it means “even”.
usage: It attaches to nouns of time and place: “열 시까지, 내일까지, 부산까지”. The pair “N부터 N까지” gives a range (“아홉 시부터 열 시까지”). With a continuing action it is “until” (“여섯 시까지 일해요”); with a one-time action such as “내다, 오다, 끝내다” it is a deadline, “by” (“내일까지 내세요”). In “너까지” it means “even you”. After a verb the ending form is “-ㄹ 때까지” (until the time when ...). It can be followed by other particles (“까지는, 까지도”).

examples.en: Today I work until six in the evening.
Submit your homework by tomorrow.

examples.ko: 집에서 학교까지 걸어서 이십 분 걸려요.
examples.en: It takes twenty minutes on foot from home to school.
It takes about three hours by train to Busan.
What am I supposed to do if even you do not believe me?

compare.difference: “에” marks a point in time; “까지” marks the end of a stretch.

pair.en: I go to bed at ten.

compare.difference: “부터” gives the start, “까지” the end; they often come in a pair.

pitfalls.note: After a verb, use “-ㄹ 때까지”, not “까지” alone.
pitfalls.en: I waited until my friend came.

topik_tip: “N까지” is “until” for a continuing action and “by” for a one-time deadline; both appear in TOPIK.

label: honorific subject
meaning_en: The honorific subject particle: it replaces “이/가” for a person to be respected (“선생님께서, 할아버지께서”). The verb takes the honorific “-시-”.
usage: It attaches to a person noun of higher status: “선생님께서, 부모님께서, 사장님께서”. The verb is in the “-(으)시-” form (“오셨다, 하신다, 계신다”), and some words change (“계시다, 드시다, 주무시다, 말씀하시다”). It can be followed by “는/도”: “께서는, 께서도”. The honoured person as a receiver takes “께” (a different particle); as subject, “께서”. It is used in speech and writing; in casual speech “이/가” is also common with “-시-”.

examples.en: The teacher wrote on the board.
My grandfather takes a walk every morning.
The president is in a meeting now.
My parents trusted me.
The kimchi that my mother sent has arrived.

compare.difference: “이/가” is neutral; “께서” adds respect. Both go with the honorific verb.
“께서” marks who does it; “께” marks who receives it.

pair.en: I gave it to the teacher.

pitfalls.note: The verb also needs the honorific “-시-”.
“께서” is only for a person to honour.

topik_tip: Honorific subjects bring a set: “께서”, “-시-”, and the special verbs (“계시다, 드시다, 주무시다”).

label: topic or contrast
meaning_en: The topic particle “은/는”: it presents the thing the sentence is about (“as for X”), marks what is already known or generic, and sets a thing against others (contrast). In the curriculum list this row is the contrast use.
usage: After a consonant it is “은”, after a vowel “는”: “책은, 저는”. Topic: “서울은 한국의 수도입니다”. Known information: a thing mentioned before takes “은/는” (“영화를 봤어요. 영화는 재미있었어요”). Contrast: “커피는 마시지만 차는 안 마셔요”. Negatives and “에는/에서는/까지는” often carry it (“주말에는”). Compare the focus of “이/가”. In questions the topic is the item being asked about (“이름은 뭐예요?”).

examples.ko: 저는 커피는 마시지만 차는 안 마셔요.
examples.en: I drink coffee, but I do not drink tea.
Seoul is the capital of Korea.

examples.ko: 어제 영화를 봤어요. 영화는 아주 재미있었어요.
examples.en: I watched a movie yesterday. The movie was very fun.
Korean is hard, but fun.
On weekends I usually rest at home.

compare.difference: “은/는” is the topic or contrast; “이/가” is the focused subject.
“은/는” singles one thing out; “도” adds another to what was already named.

pair.en: As for coffee, I drink it.

pitfalls.note: A question word asking for identity takes “이/가”, not “은/는”.
“나” becomes “내/제” only before “가”; before “는” it stays “나/저”.

topik_tip: The contrast reading (“A, but B”) is shown by the repeated “은/는” in the two halves.

label: also, even, either
meaning_en: A particle meaning “too, also”, “even”, and, with a negative, “not even ... / not any ...”. It adds one more item to something already named.
usage: It attaches to a noun and replaces “이/가/을/를” (“저도 갔어요”), or follows other particles (“에도, 에서도, 한테도, 까지도”). Repeated, “N도 N도” means “both ... and ...”. With a question word and a negative it means “none” (“아무도, 아무것도, 어디에도, 하나도”). With a counter it stresses a small amount: “한 명도 안 왔다”. “도” can also mean “even” (“점심도 못 먹었어요”).

examples.en: I will come along too.
I was so busy today that I could not even eat lunch.

examples.ko: 이 가게는 가격도 싸고 맛도 좋아요.
examples.en: This shop's prices are low, and the food is good too.
There is no one at home.
Jisu is good at English and at Japanese.

compare.difference: “도” adds (“too”); “만” limits (“only”).
“은/는” sets one thing against others; “도” says it is included as well.

pair.en: As for coffee, I drink it.

pitfalls.note: It replaces “이/가/을/를”; it does not stack on them.
“아무도” needs a negative predicate.
pitfalls.en: There is no one at home.

topik_tip: “도” plus a negative verb (“아무도 안/못 ...”) is the “nobody/nothing” frame.

label: object marker
meaning_en: The object particle “을/를”: it marks what the action is done to: “책을 읽다, 커피를 마시다”. It also marks the place passed through or left (“길을 건너다, 학교를 졸업하다”) and verbal nouns before “하다” (“공부를 하다”).
usage: After a consonant it is “을”, after a vowel “를”: “밥을, 커피를”. In speech it is often dropped (“밥 먹었어?”) or contracted (“나를 → 날”, “저를 → 절”). With “좋아하다, 싫어하다, 사랑하다” the object takes “을/를”, while with the adjectives “좋다, 싫다, 필요하다” the thing takes “이/가”. For “되다” and “아니다” the complement takes “이/가”. After motion verbs, “을/를” marks a path or a place left (“길을 건너다”, “집을 나서다”) and sometimes the destination in speech (“학교를 가다”), though “에” is the standard marker for a destination.

examples.en: I drink coffee every morning.
Jisu sang a song.
Be careful when you cross the crosswalk.
I am studying Korean.
I met a friend yesterday.

compare.difference: “을/를” marks the object of an action; “이/가” marks the subject or the thing described by an adjective.
“책을 읽었어요” is a plain statement; “책은 읽었어요” sets the book against other things.

pair.en: As for the book, I read it.

pitfalls.note: The thing wanted or liked as an adjective takes “이/가”; with the verb “좋아하다” it takes “을/를”.
The complement of “되다” takes “이/가”.

topik_tip: “좋아하다” takes “을/를” and “좋다” takes “이/가”: this pair is a classic.

label: with, and (spoken)
meaning_en: A spoken particle for “with” and “and”: “친구랑 영화를 봤어요” (with a friend), “사과랑 배” (apples and pears). It is the casual counterpart of “과/와” and “하고”.
usage: After a consonant it is “이랑”, after a vowel “랑”: “동생이랑, 친구랑, 나랑”. It marks a partner (“나랑 같이 갈래?”), a list (“김밥이랑 라면을 먹었어요”), and a comparison (“이것이랑 같아요”). It is casual speech; in writing or in a formal talk “과/와” or “하고” is used. For listing, the last noun may carry “랑” too (“사과랑 배랑 포도랑”).

examples.en: I watched a movie with a friend yesterday.
I like apples and pears.
I go to school with my younger sibling.
For lunch I ate gimbap and ramen.
Do you want to go with me?

compare.difference: “이랑” and “하고” are close in speech. “하고” is the more neutral of the two and does not change after a vowel or consonant.
“과/와” is the written form. It sounds stiff in casual talk.

pair.en: I went together with a friend.
I went together with a friend.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel it is “랑”, not “이랑”.
It is a spoken form; a formal report uses “과/와”.
pitfalls.en: Today I will present on the economies of Korea and Japan.

label: direction, means, role
meaning_en: A particle with several related jobs: direction (“학교로 가다”), means or tool (“지하철로 가다, 펜으로 쓰다, 한국어로 말하다”), material (“나무로 만들다”), role or status (“의사로 일하다”), and cause (“병으로 쉬다”).
usage: After a consonant it is “으로”, after a vowel or ㄹ it is “로”: “집으로, 손으로, 학교로, 서울로, 연필로, 지하철로”. Direction: movement toward, not necessarily arriving. Means: a vehicle, tool or language. Material: what something is made from. Role: “으로 일하다, 으로 지내다”. In “으로 정하다/결정하다” it marks the thing chosen.

examples.en: I commute by subway every day.
This cake is made with rice flour.
The class is conducted in Korean.
I am on my way home.
Jisu works as a doctor.

compare.difference: “에” names the goal where one arrives; “(으)로” names the direction one heads in.
“에서” marks where one comes from (or where an action takes place); “로” marks where one goes.

pitfalls.note: A noun ending in ㄹ takes “로”.
After a consonant other than ㄹ it is “으로”.

topik_tip: Pick “으로” or “로” by the last sound of the noun: ㄹ and vowels give “로”, other consonants give “으로”.

label: from (start of time or order)
meaning_en: A particle for a starting point: “from, starting at”, in time (“아홉 시부터”), in order (“밥부터 먹다”), and in a range with “까지”. It also marks what comes first: “먼저 ... 부터”.
usage: It attaches to nouns of time, number or order: “아침부터, 월요일부터, 처음부터, 어디부터”. “N부터 N까지” expresses a range. With the verb “시작하다” it names when something starts. For a place of origin the standard particle is “에서” (“서울에서 왔어요”). In “밥부터 먹자” it means “let's start with eating”, and “부터” can be followed by “는” (“오늘부터는”).

examples.en: Class starts at nine.
From tomorrow I will exercise every day.
I go to school from Monday to Friday.
Let's eat first and then talk.
Where shall we start reading together?

compare.difference: “부터” is a start in time or order; “에서” is a start in place.

pair.en: I have been walking since morning.

compare.difference: “에” puts something at one point in time; “부터” gives the point from which it continues.

pitfalls.note: A place of origin takes “에서”.
It is attached directly, with no “에” in front.

topik_tip: The frame “N부터 N까지” (from ... to ...) is among the first patterns tested.

label: at, to, on (time, place, target)
meaning_en: A particle with several basic jobs: a point in time (“세 시에”), the place where something exists or one is going (“책상 위에, 학교에”), a target of an action on a thing (“꽃에 물을 주다”), a cause (“바람에 쓰러지다”) and a rate (“하루에 세 번”).
usage: It attaches to nouns. Time: clock times, days, months and seasons (“일곱 시에, 월요일에, 겨울에”); the words “오늘, 어제, 내일, 지금, 언제, 그때” do not take “에”. Existence and destination: “집에 있다, 학교에 가다, 서울에 살다”. Target: for a thing or place that receives (“꽃에 물을 주다, 벽에 그림을 걸다”); a person receives “에게/한테”. Rate: “하루에 세 번, 한 개에 천 원”. For a place where an action happens, “에서” is used.

examples.en: I get up at seven in the morning.
I meet a friend on the weekend.
There is a book on the desk.
I am going to school tomorrow.
Take the medicine three times a day.
I watered the flowers.

compare.difference: “에” names where something is or where one goes; “에서” names where an action happens.
“에” marks a thing or place that receives; “에게” marks a person or animal.

pair.en: I gave water to the flowers.
I gave a present to my friend.

pitfalls.note: “어제, 오늘, 내일, 지금” take no “에”.
A verb of existence takes “에”, not “에서”.

topik_tip: “에” (point in time, place of existence, destination) versus “에서” (place of action) is the most tested particle contrast at this level.

label: to (a person or animal)
meaning_en: A particle for the person or animal that receives an action or is its target: “친구에게 선물을 주다, 동생에게 전화하다”. It is the written and neutral form of the spoken “한테”.
usage: It attaches to a person or animal noun: “친구에게, 어머니에게, 강아지에게”. Verbs: “주다, 보내다, 말하다, 묻다, 가르치다, 전화하다, 쓰다”. It also marks the source with “받다, 듣다, 배우다” (“선생님에게 칭찬을 듣다”), and the doer in a passive (“개에게 물리다”). A person to be honoured takes “께”; a thing or place takes “에”. After it, “는/도/만” can follow (“친구에게는”).

examples.en: I gave a present to my friend.
I made a phone call to my mother.
I sent a letter to Jisu.
I read a book to my younger sibling.
I was praised by the teacher.

compare.difference: “에게” and “한테” mean the same. “한테” is spoken; “에게” is neutral and also fits writing.
“에게” is for a person or animal; “에” is for a thing or place.

pair.en: I gave my younger sibling some water.

pitfalls.note: A place takes “에”, not “에게”.
A plant or a thing takes “에”.

topik_tip: The honorific partner is “께”; the spoken partner is “한테”; the source version is “에게서”.

label: at (action), from (origin)
meaning_en: A particle with two main jobs: the place where an action happens (“도서관에서 공부하다”) and the place something comes from or starts (“한국에서 왔다, 부산에서 서울까지”). With a group as the subject it works like “이/가” (“회사에서 발표했다”).
usage: It attaches to place nouns: “집에서, 학교에서, 서울에서”. Action: “공부하다, 만나다, 일하다, 먹다”. Origin and range: “오다, 출발하다, 나오다” and “N에서 N까지”. A group or institution as subject: “정부에서, 학교에서, 회사에서”. For a place of existence the particle is “에” (“집에 있다”); for a person as the source it is “에게서/한테서”. “서울에 살다” and “서울에서 살다” are both used with “살다”.

examples.en: I study in the library.
We met at school.
I went from Busan to Seoul by train.
I came from Vietnam.
The company announced a new product.

compare.difference: “에서” is where an action happens; “에” is where something is or where one goes.
“에서” marks a place as the source; “에게서” marks a person.

pair.en: A letter came from a friend.

pitfalls.note: The place of an action takes “에서”.
A person as the source takes “에게서”, not “에서”.
pitfalls.en: I received a present from a friend.

topik_tip: Remember the pair “에 있다” (be at) and “에서 -하다” (do at).

label: possessive “of, 's”
meaning_en: A particle linking two nouns: possession (“친구의 가방”), part of (“책의 제목”), relation or origin (“한국의 수도, 어머니의 사랑”). It is pronounced like “에” in speech, and often left out.
usage: It attaches to the first noun: “N의 N”. With pronouns it contracts: “나의 → 내, 저의 → 제, 너의 → 네” (“제 가방, 내 친구”); “우리의” becomes “우리” without it. In compounds a noun used as a classifier takes no “의” (“한국 음식, 학교 친구”). The particle is written “의” though in ordinary speech it is pronounced like “에”. It is not attached to verbs or adjectives; those use modifier endings.

examples.en: This is my friend's bag.
Seoul is the capital of Korea.
Today's weather in Seoul is clear.
A parent's love has no end.
My hobby is taking photos.

compare.difference: “저의” and “제” are the same; “제” is the contracted form that is usual in speech.
A noun that describes the type needs no “의”. “의” expresses belonging or relation.

pair.en: We introduce the food of Korea.

pitfalls.note: The particle is spelled “의”, even though it is pronounced like “에”.
“내, 제, 네” already contain the possessive: do not add “의”.

topik_tip: Possessive pronouns contract (“제, 내, 네”) and then take no “의”.

label: and; with (neutral spoken)
meaning_en: A particle that joins nouns (“A and B”) and marks a partner or a standard of comparison (“with”). It is the neutral spoken form, between the casual “이랑” and the written “과/와”.
usage: It attaches to any noun, with no change after a vowel or a consonant: “사과하고 배, 친구하고 같이, 이것하고 저것”. Listing: “N하고 N”. Partner: “친구하고 만나다, 선생님하고 이야기하다”. Comparison: “N하고 같다/다르다”. The speaker can also place it after the last noun (“사과하고 배하고”). It does not mark the receiver of a gift or message: that is “에게/한테”.

examples.en: I like apples and pears.
I had lunch together with a friend.
This and that are very different.
Today I went to the market with Mom.
I decided after talking with the teacher.

compare.difference: “하고” and “이랑” are near-synonyms in speech; “이랑” is more casual.
“과/와” is the written form and sounds stiff in casual speech.

pair.en: I bought a book and a notebook.
I bought a book and a notebook.

pitfalls.note: It means “with” or “and”, not “to”: the receiver of a gift takes “에게/한테”.
pitfalls.en: I gave my friend a present.

topik_tip: Do not confuse the particle “하고” with the verb “하다” + “-고”: it joins nouns.

label: only, just that one
meaning_en: A particle meaning “only, just”: it limits something to one thing and excludes the rest. It can also stress a minimum (“한 번만”).
usage: It attaches to a noun, a counter phrase, an adverb or another particle: “커피만, 두 명만, 집에서만, 너에게만”. It replaces “이/가/을/를” (“저만 갔어요”, “커피만 마셔요”) and sits after others (“에서만, 에게만”). It goes with positive and negative predicates alike. For “only + a negative verb” the particle “밖에” is used; for “only” at the end of a sentence “뿐이다”. “이번만” means “just this once”.

examples.en: I only drink coffee.
Only two students were in the classroom.
Today I rested only at home.

examples.ko: 이 일은 지수만 할 수 있어요.
examples.en: Only Jisu can do this job.
Please help me, just this once.

compare.difference: “만” limits (“only”); “도” adds (“too”).
“만” goes with a positive or negative verb. “밖에” needs a negative and suggests the amount is small.

pitfalls.note: “만” replaces “을/를”; it does not stand next to it.

topik_tip: “만” (any predicate), “밖에” (negative predicate) and “뿐” (with “이다”) are three ways to say only.

label: to (a person), spoken
meaning_en: The spoken form of “에게”: it marks the person or animal that receives an action: “친구한테 전화하다”. It also marks the source with “받다/듣다” and the doer in a passive (“선생님한테 혼나다”).
usage: It attaches to a person or animal: “친구한테, 엄마한테, 강아지한테”. Verbs: “주다, 말하다, 묻다, 보내다, 전화하다, 가르치다”; “받다, 듣다, 배우다” for a source (“친구한테 선물을 받았어요”); a passive doer (“혼나다, 잡히다, 물리다”). A source can also take “한테서”. It is colloquial; in writing “에게” is used. A thing or a place takes “에”, and an honoured person “께”.

examples.en: I called Mom yesterday.
I received a present from a friend.
I fed the puppy.
I got scolded by the teacher yesterday.
Who did you hear that story from?

compare.difference: The two have the same meaning; “에게” is neutral and also used in writing.
“께” replaces “한테/에게” for a person to be honoured.

pair.en: I gave it to my younger sibling.
I gave it to my grandmother.

pitfalls.note: A plant or a thing takes “에”.

topik_tip: In listening items “한테” and “에게” are interchangeable; “께” signals an honoured person.

label: than (comparison)
meaning_en: A particle for the standard of a comparison: “A는 B보다 ...” means “A is more ... than B”. It is often combined with “더” (“more”) or “훨씬” (“much”).
usage: It attaches to the thing that is compared against: “부산보다, 어제보다, 생각보다, 저보다”. The predicate is a comparable adjective or adverb: “크다, 많다, 빠르다, 좋아하다”. Frames: “A가 B보다 더 ...”, “B보다 A를 더 좋아하다”. “생각보다” (than I thought) and “기대보다” (than expected) are frequent set phrases. Equal comparisons use “만큼” or “처럼”. “보다” can also be an adverb meaning “more” (“보다 좋은 방법”).

examples.en: Seoul has a larger population than Busan.
Today is colder than yesterday.
I like tea more than coffee.
This bag is much lighter than I thought.
My younger sibling is taller than I am.

compare.difference: “보다” says one is more; “만큼” says they are equal.

pair.en: They run as fast as Jisu.

compare.difference: As a bare adverb, “보다” means “more” and compares nothing.

pitfalls.note: It is a particle, so it is attached to the noun without a space.

topik_tip: The set phrase “생각보다” (more ... than I thought) is the most frequent form.

label: will; must be; polite softener
meaning_en: A pre-final ending with three jobs: the speaker's will (“제가 하겠습니다”), a guess about the present or the future (“비가 오겠어요, 힘들겠어요”), and a polite softening in set phrases (“처음 뵙겠습니다, 알겠습니다, 모르겠습니다”).
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems and sits before the final ending: “하다 → 하겠다”, “맛있다 → 맛있겠다”. With the speaker as subject it is a decision made now (“제가 가겠습니다”). With others it is a guess (“그 사람은 지금 바쁘겠어요”). It does not point to the past: a past guess is “-었겠-” (“어제 힘들었겠어요”). Questions “-겠어요?” ask about the listener's will or about a guess. It is typical in “합쇼체” (“-겠습니다”).

examples.en: I will do the dishes today.
Looking at the sky, it will rain soon.
The exam is tomorrow, so you must be very nervous.
Nice to meet you. I look forward to your help.
I do not quite know. Please explain it again.
This food looks really delicious.

compare.difference: “-겠-” voices a decision at the moment of speaking; “-을 거예요” states a plan or a prediction.

pair.en: I am going to do it.

compare.difference: “-겠습니다” is the formal declaration; “-을게요” is the everyday promise.

pitfalls.note: “-겠-” does not mark the past: use “-었겠-” for a guess about the past.
pitfalls.en: It must have been very hard yesterday.

topik_tip: “알겠습니다 / 모르겠습니다 / 처음 뵙겠습니다” are polite formulas, not predictions.
